title: Why compound interest wins
blurb: Interest lands on top of interest, so money grows faster the longer it sits. You'll see what $1,000 does at 8% a year, and the one-line trick for knowing when it doubles.
takeaway: You learned why time matters more than amount.

cards.body: Compound interest means you earn interest on your interest. Like a snowball rolling downhill, the money grows faster the longer it goes.
Put $1,000 in an account paying 8% a year. Twelve months later it has grown by $80. Nothing clever yet. That is just the rate doing its job.
Year 2 you earn $86, not $80. The $80 from last year is sitting in the account now, so it earns interest too. That extra $6 is the whole trick.
Leave it alone. Year 10 it’s $2,159. Year 20, $4,661. Year 30, over $10,000. All from $1,000 you never touched.
A flat $80 a year would give you $3,400 after 30 years. Interest on interest gives you $10,063. That gap is compounding.
Divide 72 by the rate to see how long doubling takes. At 8%, that’s 9 years: $1,000, $2,000, $4,000, $8,000.
Two people both put away $200 a month, every month, into the same kind of account. One starts at 18. The other waits and starts at 28.
By 60, the one who started at 18 has about $824,000. The one who started at 28 has about $355,000.
The early saver only put in $24,000 more. Time did the rest. The extra ten years let the interest pile up on itself.
Starting at 18 instead of 28 can roughly double what you end up with. Time matters more than amount.
It works against you too. Credit card debt compounds the same way, often at 25%. A small balance rolls into a big one.

cards.question: Why does year 2 earn more than year 1?
choices: You added more money to the account during the year.
The interest from year 1 is now earning interest too.
The bank raises the rate a little each year you stay.
cards.why: Interest is added to your balance, so year 2 is worked out on $1,080 instead of $1,000. Nothing else changed.

title: Your first budget in 4 lines
blurb: A budget is a plan you make before you spend, not a punishment you write after. Four lines is enough to start, and one of them does most of the work.
takeaway: You learned that the savings line should move on its own.

cards.body: A budget is a plan for money before you spend it, not a punishment you write after. Four lines is enough to start, and one of them does most of the work.
Split what comes in into four lines. Half to needs, about a third to wants, a fifth to savings. On $2,000 a month that is $1,000, $600 and $400.
Half goes to needs. Rent, food, the bus, the phone bill. Things that happen whether you plan them or not. That is the 50.
Thirty percent is wants. Eating out, the concert, the game. Not a moral failing, just a planned amount. Planned is the difference.
The last fifth is savings. That is the line that actually changes anything. $400 a month is $4,800 a year, and the first $500 of it is your emergency fund.
Track one month before you set the numbers. Most people are shocked by one category. That category is your lever. Fix that one and leave the rest alone.
Set the savings line to move on payday, by itself. If it moves first, you never have to be disciplined. What is left is what you spend, and you cannot overspend money you never see.
Saving what is left over never works, because nothing is left over. The month always finds a use for visible money. Move it first, then live on the rest.
That is the whole budget. Four lines on a page. Check it once a month, move one number if it was wrong, and leave it alone the rest of the time.
Automate the savings line. If it moves on payday, you never have to be disciplined.

cards.question: Why automate savings instead of saving what's left over?
choices: Banks pay a better rate on automatic transfers.
Nothing is ever left over at the end of the month.
Automatic transfers raise your credit score.
cards.why: Money you can see is money you spend. Moving it first makes the plan happen without willpower.

title: What an emergency fund is for
blurb: The point of an emergency fund is not the interest. It's that a flat tyre stops being a crisis and starts being an errand.
takeaway: You learned what cash is for when something breaks.

cards.body: An emergency fund is cash you keep boring on purpose. Not invested, not locked up, not doing anything clever. Just there, for the day something breaks.
A $400 repair with the cash there is an errand. You pay it, you drive home, and you have forgotten it by the weekend.
The same $400 on a card at 24%, paying $25 a month, takes 20 months to clear and costs about $100 in interest. The flat tyre follows you into next year.
Start with $500. That covers most of what actually goes wrong: a phone screen, a tyre, a co-pay, a charger. Big disasters are rare. Small ones are monthly.
Keep it in a separate savings account, not the one you spend from. Out of sight, but one transfer away. Not invested, because the market can be down on the day the car breaks.
Once $500 is there, keep going. One month of rent and food is the next stop. Three months is the point where a lost job is a problem, not a catastrophe.
The fund is not about the interest it earns. It is about the loans you never take. It buys you the right to say no to bad borrowing.
Using it is what it is for. When you do, the next paychecks refill it before anything else. Wants pause for a month. The fund comes back.
Most of what it buys is quiet. A noise from the car is a noise, not a spiral. That calm is worth more than the 4% the bank pays on it.
An emergency fund buys you the right to say no to bad borrowing.

cards.question: Why keep an emergency fund in plain cash instead of investing it?
choices: Cash in a savings account grows faster than stocks.
It has to be all there on the day you need it.
Investments cannot be sold in under a month.
cards.why: Investments can be down exactly when your car breaks. The job of this money is to be available, not to grow.

title: Credit scores, plainly
blurb: A credit score is a guess about whether you pay people back. Two of the five inputs do most of the work, and both are in your control.
takeaway: You learned that paying on time beats paying it all.

cards.body: A credit score is one number that guesses how likely you are to pay back what you borrow. Landlords, phone companies and banks look at it before they say yes to you.
It runs from 300 to 850. Under 580 counts as poor, 670 to 739 is good, 800 and up is exceptional. The average American sits at about 715.
Five things feed it, and two do most of the work. Paying on time is 35% of the score. How much of your limit you use is another 30%. The other three are small.
Paying on time is the heaviest input by a distance. One payment 30 days late can knock up to about 100 points off a good score, and the mark stays on your report for seven years.

Second is how much of your limit you use. With a $1,000 limit, a $300 balance is 30%. Under 30% is the usual advice. Under 10% is better, and it counts even if you pay in full, because the statement balance is what gets reported.
Length of history is 15%. That is why closing your oldest card can hurt: it shortens your record and shrinks your total limit. Keep the old card and use it once in a while.
Paying the whole balance 30 days late hurts more than paying the minimum on time. The late mark lasts seven years. A balance is gone the month you clear it.

Three companies keep the records: Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. Your bank reports to them every month. You can read your own report for free at annualcreditreport.com, and checking it never hurts your score.
Paying on time is worth more than paying it all off. One late payment costs more than a big balance.
Starting at 18 with one card, one small monthly charge, and autopay for the full balance is the whole game. By the time you need a car loan or an apartment, you will have years of on-time history.

cards.question: You can only do one this month. Which helps your score more?
choices: Pay the whole balance, 30 days late.
Pay just the minimum, but on time.
Close your oldest card to simplify.
cards.why: Payment history is the heaviest single input. A late mark sits on your report for years; a carried balance does not.

title: Good debt, bad debt
blurb: Debt isn't good or bad by nature. It's a price you pay for time, and the question is only ever whether you're buying something worth more than the price.
takeaway: You learned to ask what the debt buys before you take it.

cards.body: All debt is renting money. The interest rate is the rent. You are not buying the money, you are borrowing it for a while and paying for the time.
24% a year means if you owe $1,000 for a year, $240 of that is the fee for owing it. Nothing you bought got better. That is rent.
Rent is worth paying when the thing you bought is worth more later. A degree you finish. A van for a business that earns. The thing grows faster than the rent does.
A degree is worth it if you finish it and it leads somewhere. Debt for a course you drop out of is the same debt with none of the payoff.
It almost never is when the thing shrinks: a night out, a phone, a weekend away. You are still paying rent on it long after it is gone.
Put $1,000 on a card at 24% and pay the $25 minimum. It takes almost seven years. You pay back about $2,050. Half of that is rent on a night you already forgot.
Write them all down with their rates. Pay the minimum on every one. Then throw every spare dollar at the highest rate. That order saves the most money, every time.
Zero percent for twelve months is still debt with a deadline. Some of those charge you all the skipped interest at once if you are late or still owe anything at the end.
Before you borrow for anything, ask one question. Will this still be worth something when I finish paying for it? If the answer is no, pay cash or wait.
Ask one question: will this still be worth something when I finish paying for it?

cards.question: A credit card charges 24% a year. A savings account pays 4%. What should a spare $100 do first?
choices: Go into the savings account to earn 4%.
Pay down the card that is charging 24%.
Split evenly between the two accounts.
cards.why: Paying off 24% debt is a guaranteed 24% return. No savings account can beat that.

title: Why index funds beat picking
blurb: Most professional stock pickers lose to a fund that buys everything and thinks about nothing. Here's why that keeps happening.
takeaway: You learned why the boring fund keeps winning.

cards.body: A fund is a big bucket lots of people put money into. The bucket buys things, and you own a slice of the bucket. An index fund's rule is the simplest one there is: buy everything on the list, then leave it alone.
An index fund buys a slice of every company on a list. The S&P 500 list has 500 of them. You do not have to know which one will win, because you own a bit of all of them.
Picking one company means being right about that one, twice, for twenty years. Right when you buy and right when you sell. Full-time professionals are paid to do exactly this.
Over twenty years, about nine in ten professional stock pickers land behind the boring fund. Fees and bad timing eat the difference. That is not a bad year. It is the usual result.
Fees sound tiny and are not. Put $10,000 in for twenty years at 7% and you end up with about $38,700. Charge 1% a year in fees and it is about $32,100. That 1% quietly took $6,600.
When you look at a fund, find the expense ratio. That is the yearly fee. Broad index funds are often under 0.1%. Anything over 1% needs to explain itself.
The other mistake is checking it. The fund will drop, sometimes a lot. Selling then is how you lock the loss in. The boring plan only works if you are boring about it.
Every crash is a dent in a line that goes up. The people who lost money were the ones who sold in the dent. The line did not need them to do anything.
Pick one broad index fund. Set a monthly amount to move into it on payday. Then close the app and go live your life. Checking it is the only way to mess it up.
The boring fund wins because it costs almost nothing and never panics.

cards.question: Why do fees matter so much over 20 years?
choices: Fees go up a little every year you stay invested.
Fees come out of money that would have compounded.
Fees get taxed twice, once now and once later.
cards.why: Every dollar in fees is a dollar that stops earning. Over decades a 1% fee quietly takes a large slice of the total.

title: Stoicism: control what you can
blurb: The Stoics split the world in two and told you to spend your energy on one half. It's two thousand years old and it maps almost exactly onto a bad exam week.
takeaway: You learned to spend your energy on the half you control.

cards.body: The Stoics were Greek and Roman thinkers two thousand years ago. Their first move was to split the world in two: the things you control, and the things you do not.
Your effort and your reaction are in the first group. Those are always yours. A posted grade, a curve, what somebody else scored: all second group.
Epictetus was born a slave and walked with a limp all his life. He had less control over his own life than almost anyone. He said suffering comes from trying to control the second group.
A grade is already up. Refreshing the page is second group. Emailing to ask what you missed is first group. Same evening, two very different uses of it.

Worry is energy spent on the second group. It feels like doing something and changes nothing on the page. The Stoics were not calm because nothing bothered them. They were calm because they moved the energy.
The Stoics used an archer. The archer controls the aim, the breathing, the release. Once the arrow is gone, the wind owns it. Do your part well, then let it fly.
You do not control the traffic. You control whether you spend the twenty minutes furious or listening to something. The event is second group. Your reaction is first.
The whole practice fits in one question. Before you stress, ask: is this in my control? If no, let it go. If yes, do the next step today.
Tonight, list what is worrying you. Cross out everything in the second group. What is left is your to-do list. It is usually shorter than the worry was.
Before you stress, ask: is this in my control? If no, let it go. If yes, act on it today.

cards.question: Which of these is in the first group, the part you control?
choices: The curve the professor puts on the test.
How many hours you put in before the test.
What your friend ended up scoring on it.
cards.why: Your effort is yours. The curve and other people's scores are outcomes you can influence at best, never control.

title: The Socratic method
blurb: Socrates never told anyone the answer. He asked until they noticed they didn't have one. It turns out that is the fastest way to find out what you actually know.
takeaway: You learned that asking why beats reading again.

cards.body: Socrates taught by asking questions, not giving answers. He wrote nothing down. His method was to keep asking people to explain what they had just said, until it held up or it didn't.
Start with something you believe. Ask why once and you get a reason. That part is usually easy. Ask why again, and again, and most beliefs run out of floor.
'I should use flashcards.' Why? 'Because they help me remember.' Why do they? 'Because I test myself.' Why does testing work? Three questions in, you either know or you have found the hole.
Running out of floor is not a failure. That is the method working. The spot where you cannot answer is the exact spot worth studying.
It feels bad, and it is supposed to. Finding out you cannot explain something you were sure about is uncomfortable. That discomfort is the only reliable sign you found something worth learning.
Cover the page and ask why the answer is the answer. If you can only say what the answer is, you memorised a shape and not an idea.
This is a tool for checking your own thinking, not for winning arguments. Asking someone why five times in a row does not make you Socrates. It makes you annoying.
Athens put Socrates on trial in 399 BC for corrupting the young with questions. He kept asking them at the trial. His students wrote the questions down, and we are still asking them.
A test never asks you to recognise the answer. It asks you to produce it, with the reason attached. Asking why is practising exactly that.
Asking why this is the answer beats rereading the answer.

cards.question: Why does asking 'why' beat rereading your notes?
choices: It takes far less time than reading them all again.
It makes you produce the reason instead of see it.
Notes are usually wrong somewhere in the first place.
cards.why: Recognising something feels like knowing it. Producing the reason from memory is the thing a test actually asks for.

title: Occam's razor
blurb: The oldest debugging tool there is: when two explanations both fit, start with the one that assumes less. It isn't a law of nature, and that matters too.
takeaway: You learned which explanation to test first.

cards.body: Occam's razor: when two explanations fit the same facts, start with the one that assumes less. It is the oldest debugging tool there is, and it is seven hundred years old.

It is named after William of Ockham, a friar in England in the 1300s. He argued you should not invent extra things to explain something if you do not need them. A razor, because it shaves off what you do not need.
Your code broke right after you changed one line. Two explanations fit: you typed something wrong, or the compiler has a bug that nobody else has ever hit.
Count what each one needs to be true. 'I typed it wrong' needs one thing. 'The compiler is broken' needs four: a bug exists, nobody has found it, it lives in your line, and it only showed up today.
So the razor is an order, not an answer. Check the cheap one first. If it holds, you are done in a minute. If it does not, you lost a minute and you now know something.

The common misuse is treating simplest as truest. Sometimes the weird explanation is the real one. The razor does not say it is wrong. It says check the boring one before you spend a day on the interesting one.
Doctors learn the same rule as a saying: when you hear hoofbeats, think horses, not zebras. A headache is usually a headache. They still check for zebras when the horses do not explain it.
Try it the next time something breaks. Write the two explanations down. Count what each one needs to be true. Test the smaller number first, every time.
Nine times in ten it was the typo. The tenth time, you have already ruled out the cheap answer, so the expensive hunt is worth it. Either way, you started in the right place.
The simplest explanation isn't the truest. It's the one worth checking first.

cards.question: What does the razor actually tell you to do?
choices: Believe the simplest answer and stop there.
Test the simplest answer before the others.
Ignore any answer that sounds complicated.
cards.why: It ranks what to check, not what is true. A complicated explanation can still win once the simple one fails.

title: The veil of ignorance
blurb: John Rawls' test for whether a rule is fair: design it before you know who you'll be under it.
takeaway: You learned a test for whether a rule is actually fair.

cards.body: John Rawls asked: what rules would you write for a society if you did not know who you would be in it? Rich or poor, healthy or sick, born here or far away.
You keep everything you know about how the world works. You lose only who you are in it. Your money, your health, your talents, your family. All behind the veil.
Then you get handed a life at random and have to live under the rules you just wrote. If you wrote them for the lucky, you might be the unlucky. So you write them for everyone.
A fair rule is one you would still write if you did not know which side of it you would land on. That is the whole test, and it works on rules of any size.
Would you set the late-work policy the same way if you did not know whether you would be the student with a job after school? Probably not. Now you know what to change.
'No late work, ever' is a great rule if you know you will never need it. 'One late pass a term' is the one you write when you might. The veil picks the second.
Rawls was a Harvard philosopher. His 1971 book A Theory of Justice made the veil famous. He argued fair rules are the ones people would agree to before they knew their luck.
It is the grown-up version of a rule every kid knows: one cuts the cake, the other picks the slice. The cutter cuts fairly because they do not know which piece they will get.
Next time you make a rule for a group, ask who ends up worst off under it. Then ask if you would take that seat. If not, the rule is not finished.
A fair rule is one you'd still write if you didn't know which side of it you'd land on.

cards.question: What is the veil hiding from you?
choices: The consequences the rule will have on others.
Which position in society you will end up in.
Who else is voting on the same rule as you.
cards.why: You keep full knowledge of how the world works. You lose only the knowledge of who you'll be in it.

title: The map is not the territory
blurb: Every model leaves things out on purpose. Trouble starts when you forget which things.
takeaway: You learned to ask what a model left out.

cards.body: A map is useful because it leaves things out. A map with everything on it would be the size of the world, and no use to anyone trying to get home.
The map keeps the road and drops the potholes. That is the deal. Every useful picture of the world is a smaller, simpler thing that stands in for it.
Every model does this: a formula, a stereotype, a study guide. Something got cut to make it usable. The formula drops friction. The stereotype drops the person.
A subway map is famously wrong about distances. Stations look evenly spaced when they are not. It is wrong on purpose, because the thing you need is the order of the stops.
A practice test predicts your real score well. It still cannot tell you that you always slow down on the last section. That detail got cut, and it is the one you needed.
People drive into lakes following a GPS. The map said road. The territory said water. Trusting the map over your own eyes is how it happens.
The skill is not distrusting maps. It is knowing what was cut, and whether you needed it. Two questions, asked before you trust what a model says.
A stereotype is a map of a person drawn before you met them. It can be handy for a stranger in a hurry. It is useless for a friend, because everything you like about them is what it cut.
Alfred Korzybski, a Polish-American thinker, said it in 1931: the map is not the territory. His point was that words and models are tools for the world, not the world itself.
Ask what a model left out before you trust what it says.

cards.question: What makes a map useful?
choices: It shows everything that is really out there.
It leaves out the right things for the job.
It never has to change once it is drawn.
cards.why: Detail is what makes a map unusable. The skill is knowing which detail was dropped and whether you needed it.

title: Spaced practice beats cramming
blurb: Same total hours, very different results. Splitting study across days works because forgetting a little is part of how remembering gets strong.
takeaway: You learned that the gap between sessions does the work.

cards.body: The night before a test, one long cram. Three hours, one desk, one energy drink. It all goes in fast, and it feels like it is working.
And it leaks just as fast. By the next morning some of it is already gone. A week later, most of what you crammed has gone with it.
Spacing means splitting the time you were going to spend anyway. Not more hours. The same hour, cut into pieces, with days between them.
Split the same hour over six days. Each ten-minute session catches the memory just before it slips, and lifts it a little higher than last time.
Your brain strengthens a memory each time it nearly forgets it, then pulls it back. A memory you never have to reach for stays weak.
Cramming feels better and works worse. When it's all fresh, recalling is easy, so you feel like you know it. The ease is the problem.
Put the sessions in your calendar the day you get the material. Ten minutes each, a day apart. If it is not on the calendar, it will not happen.
This lesson can't save you tonight. If the test is tomorrow, cram, then get some sleep. Space the next one and feel the difference.
Anything you have to remember: vocab, formulas, dates, names. It also works for skills like problem sets, as long as you spread the practice out.
The gap between sessions is doing the work, not the sessions.

cards.question: Why does leaving a gap between study sessions help?
choices: You come back rested, so you can focus for longer.
Partly forgetting makes each recall count for more.
Shorter sessions are easier to fit into a busy week.
cards.why: Rest and fit are nice, but they are not the mechanism. Each time you nearly forget and pull it back, the memory gets stronger.

title: How to study for a science quiz
blurb: Science quizzes ask you to explain a mechanism, not to recognise a term. Three passes over two evenings does more than one long night with a highlighter.
takeaway: You learned to draw the mechanism instead of highlighting it.

cards.body: A science quiz almost never asks you to recognise a word. Highlighting the definition feels like work and isn't. Your eyes did something. Your memory did not.
Draw the mechanism instead. Osmosis: two sides, which one is saltier, and which way the water goes. Three marks on a page, and you own the idea.
If you can draw it from memory, you can answer any wording of the question. 'Which way does water move?' 'What happens to the cell?' 'Why does the slug shrivel?' Same drawing.

Do not memorise 'osmosis: movement of water'. Close the book, draw the two sides, mark the saltier one, then draw the arrow. If the arrow goes the wrong way, you just found the thing you did not know.
Two evenings before the quiz. Night one: write and draw what you remember, then check. Night two: redraw only the gaps. Rereading the chapter is not on the list.
Almost every science topic is a mechanism with a direction. Photosynthesis. A circuit. The water cycle. If there is an arrow in it, draw it.
In the quiz, draw the picture in the margin before you write a word. The drawing answers the question. The words just report what the drawing says.
You are ready when you can draw it, label it, say which way it goes and say why. Four checks, no highlighter.
Salt on a slug pulls the water out of it. That is osmosis with a direction, and you will never forget it. Facts with a picture stay. Definitions leave.
If you can draw the mechanism from memory, you're ready. Highlighting is not studying.

cards.question: You have two evenings before the quiz. What's the better use of night one?
choices: Reread the chapter carefully from the start.
Write and draw what you remember, then check.
Make a colour-coded summary sheet of terms.
cards.why: Writing it first shows you the gaps. Rereading shows you familiar pages and hides what you don't know.

title: Active recall in ten minutes
blurb: The single highest-value ten minutes in studying, and it needs no app, no cards, and no colour coding.
takeaway: You learned to start with a blank page, every time.

cards.body: Active recall means pulling something out of your head, not putting it back in. The blank page does the pulling. It is the highest-value ten minutes in studying.
There is a difference between knowing something and recognising it. You recognise a face you cannot name. Rereading trains recognising. Exams ask you to name.
The whole method is three steps. Close everything. Write what you remember on a blank page. Open the notes and mark what was not there.
Ten minutes, for real. Two minutes shutting the laptop and the notes. Five minutes writing everything you can remember. Three minutes opening the notes and marking what you missed.
The part you missed is your entire study list. Everything else is already learned. Most people study the whole chapter again. You only need the gaps.
Rereading fools people. It feels smooth and quick, and that smoothness gets mistaken for knowing. A blank page feels awful because it is actually measuring you.
You do not need anything for it. Walking to class, try to list the four things from the last lecture. Whatever you cannot get is what you open the notes for later.
In a famous 2006 study, students who reread a passage four times remembered 40% of it a week later. Students who read it once and then tested themselves three times remembered 61%.
The mistake is checking too early. If you peek the second it gets hard, you have turned it back into reading. Sit in the blank for a bit. That struggle is the part that works.
Blank page first, notes second. Always in that order.

cards.question: Rereading your notes feels much easier than a blank page. Why is that a warning sign?
choices: Easy means it has already gone into long-term memory.
Recognising is easier than recalling, and tests need recall.
Notes are shorter than the textbook, so they read faster.
cards.why: Familiarity feels like knowledge. A blank page is uncomfortable precisely because it measures the thing a test measures.

title: Mix the problems up
blurb: Doing twenty of the same problem type teaches you to run one method. Mixing them teaches you to pick one, which is the harder half.
takeaway: You learned to practise choosing the method, not just running it.

cards.body: Most problem sets are blocked: four of type A, then four of type B. By the third one you are not thinking. You are running the same method again.
Blocked trains running a method. Mixed trains choosing one, which is the harder half. On a mixed page, every problem starts with 'what kind is this?'
On the test nothing is labelled. The section heading that told you which method to use is gone. Practise the part that isn't labelled.
Do 5 of A and 5 of B to learn the moves. Then shuffle 10 together and do those. The shuffled ten are where the test actually lives.
In a 2007 study, students who practised blocked got 89% right in practice and 20% on the test a week later. The mixed group got 60% in practice and 63% on the test.
Mixed practice feels worse while you do it. You make more mistakes, because choosing is the skill being built. The mistakes are the training, not a sign it is not working.
Before you solve anything, say what kind of problem it is and how you know. Out loud if you can. That one sentence is the skill the test is checking.
Coaches have known for years. A tennis player who practises forehands for an hour looks great and loses. One who gets random serves looks worse in practice and wins.
Learn each type on its own first. Then every session after that is mixed. If your textbook does not mix them, you do it yourself with a bowl and some slips.
On the test nothing is labelled. Practise the part that isn't labelled.

cards.question: Why does mixed practice feel worse than blocked practice?
choices: It takes longer to get through the same page.
You make more mistakes while learning to choose.
The problems in a mixed set are harder ones.
cards.why: Struggling to pick the right method is the skill being built. The mistakes are the training, not a sign it isn't working.

title: How to read a chapter once
blurb: Reading a chapter twice is usually reading it badly once, twice. Three moves make one pass enough.
takeaway: You learned to read once, with a question in hand.

cards.body: Most people read a chapter, remember nothing, and read it again. Reading with no question is moving your eyes over a page and hoping. Twice.
Before reading, turn every heading into a question. 'Cell division' becomes 'how does a cell divide?' Six headings become six questions. That is the whole setup.
A question gives your brain something to look for. Now you are searching for an answer instead of scanning a page, and you notice it when it arrives.
Do it out loud with the contents page first. It takes about two minutes and it is the whole setup. Everything after that is just reading with a purpose.
When you finish, shut the book and write four sentences. That is your whole set of notes. Four from memory beats two pages of copying.
If the book is open you will copy, and copying feels like working while teaching you nothing. Shut is the important word.
If a section has no headings, use the first line of each paragraph instead. Same trick. You are looking for what this bit is trying to tell me.
A highlighter marks what looked important while you were reading. That is a decision you make before you understand anything. It leaves you a yellow page and no answers.
Questions first. Read once, looking for the answers. Shut the book. Write four sentences. Open it and check. One pass, and you can say what the chapter said.
Reading twice is slower than reading once and answering.

cards.question: Why turn headings into questions before you read?
choices: It makes the chapter shorter to get through.
It gives you something to be looking for.
Questions are easier to remember than titles.
cards.why: A question turns reading from scanning into searching. You notice the answer when it arrives, instead of noticing nothing.

title: The five-minute start
blurb: Procrastination is nearly always about starting, not about working. So make starting the only thing you commit to.
takeaway: You learned to commit to starting and let finishing follow.

cards.body: Putting something off is almost always about starting it, not about doing it. The task is fine. The doorway is the problem.
The hard part is the first minute, not the next forty. Once you are in, the work carries itself along. The wall is at the door.
So shrink the commitment to five minutes, and mean the part where you are allowed to stop. Five real minutes, then a real choice.
Set an actual timer. Open the file. Do the ugliest first step you can think of. When it rings, you are free to leave, and you will not want to.
Most of the time you do not stop. Starting was the hard part and it is behind you. The five minutes were never the job. They were the door.
For an essay, the five minutes is opening the file and writing a bad first sentence. Bad is fine. It gets deleted. Its job was to exist.
If the five minutes is a trick, your brain stops falling for it. The method works because starting is genuinely cheap. Make stopping allowed, every time.
The timer rang half an hour ago. You did not hear it. That is not discipline. That is what happens once the door is behind you.
Every task has a five-minute version. An essay: one bad sentence. A problem set: copy out question one. A chapter: turn the first heading into a question.
Commit to starting, never to finishing. Finishing takes care of itself more often than you'd think.

cards.question: Why does the five minutes have to be a real permission to stop?
choices: Five minutes is enough time for most tasks.
If it is a trick, your brain stops falling for it.
It keeps every study session short and tidy.
cards.why: The method works because starting is genuinely cheap. If stopping isn't allowed, starting costs the whole task again.

title: Your brain holds about four things
blurb: Working memory is the scratchpad you think with, and it is tiny. You'll see why a phone on the desk costs you a slot, and the one trick that makes four slots feel like more.
takeaway: You learned why one open tab is a study tool.

cards.body: Working memory is the scratchpad you think with. It holds about four things at once, and that is it. Every thought you are holding right now is sitting on that pad.
Every open loop takes a slot. The song stuck in your head. The text you have not answered. The phone face up on the desk. That is three of four gone before you start.
When a fifth thing arrives, something falls off. It is usually the thing you were trying to learn, because it is the newest and the least practised.
A phone face up on the desk keeps a slot busy even when it is silent. Part of you is waiting for it. Face down in a bag is a different object.
The trick is chunking: pack several items into one. 8675309 is seven things. 867-5309 is two. A phone number fits because you learned to chunk it.
Before a problem set, write the three formulas on a sticky note. Now they live on paper, and the slots are free for the actual problem.
Every open tab is a promise to come back, and each promise takes a slot. Close all but the one you are using. One tab is not a style choice. It is a study tool.
In 1956 George Miller put the number at seven, plus or minus two. Later work by Nelson Cowan settled on about four for new, unchunked items. Seven was the number for things you had already chunked.
Before you start, write down everything you are carrying: the text to answer, the errand, the worry. On paper it stops taking a slot. This is why a to-do list feels like relief.
Four slots. Everything you carry in your head is sitting in one of them.

cards.question: Why does a phone face up on the desk hurt studying?
choices: The screen light makes it harder to read the page.
It keeps a slot busy even when it makes no sound.
It only hurts if a notification actually buzzes.
cards.why: An unfinished thing stays open in your head. It sits in a slot whether or not the phone makes a sound.

title: Why you can't stop scrolling
blurb: Feeds are built on the same trick as slot machines: a reward that only sometimes comes. You'll see why 'sometimes' hooks harder than 'always', and the one setting that breaks the loop.
takeaway: You learned that 'sometimes' is the hook.

cards.body: Pull down to refresh. Something might be there. Something might not. That uncertainty is the whole design, and it was designed on purpose.
Most pulls give you nothing. Then one gives you a like, a reply, a good post. You keep pulling for the next one, because the next one might be it.
A reward that comes every time gets boring fast. A reward that comes sometimes keeps you pulling longest. Slot machines run on exactly this.
A slot machine pays out on a random schedule too. The design is the same: a pull, a pause, and a maybe. Feeds borrowed it because it works.
Pigeons taught to peck for a seed every time stopped when the seed stopped. Pigeons rewarded at random kept pecking for hours. B. F. Skinner ran this in the 1950s.
Every notification is a cue for a pull. The buzz says something might be there. That is the same maybe, delivered to your pocket, thirty times a day.
The fix is not willpower. Kill the surprise. With notifications off, nothing arrives unannounced, so there is no pull to answer. You check when you decide to.
Do it once. Turn off notifications for every feed app. Leave on the ones from actual people. It takes two minutes and the pull goes quiet the same day.
The first few days feel like something is missing. That is the maybe going quiet. Boredom comes back, and boredom is where your own thoughts live.
The feed isn't fun. It's uncertain. Uncertainty is what you're hooked on.

cards.question: Which reward keeps a habit going the longest?
choices: One that arrives every single time you act.
One that arrives at random, only sometimes.
One that arrives on a fixed daily schedule.
cards.why: A random reward means every pull could be the one. There's never a moment where stopping feels safe.

title: The sunk cost trap
blurb: You paid for the ticket, so you sit through the bad movie. That's the trap. You'll see why money already spent shouldn't vote, and how to catch yourself doing it.
takeaway: You learned that only the future gets a vote.

cards.body: You paid $15 for the movie. Twenty minutes in, it is bad. Really bad. You look at the exit, then back at the screen, and you stay. Why?
The $15 is gone either way. Stay or leave, you do not get it back. So the money should not get a vote. It is not on the ballot anymore.
The next 90 minutes are still yours. That is the only thing the decision is about. Would you pay 90 minutes of your evening to watch the rest of this? If not, leave.
Sunk cost is when the past votes anyway. 'I have already waited forty minutes' is the sound it makes. The more you have put in, the louder it gets.
Three semesters into a major you hate. The credits are spent. Switching does not give them back, and staying does not either. The only question is whether the next three are worth it.
Britain and France kept paying for the Concorde jet for years after it was clear it would never make its money back. Economists named the trap after it: the Concorde fallacy.
Draw a line. Everything above it is spent: money, time, effort. Everything below it is still yours. Decide using only what is below the line.
Leaving a bad movie feels like wasting $15. It is the opposite. The $15 is gone whatever you do. Walking out is the only way to save the evening.
Money and time already spent are gone in every version of the future. Only what's ahead gets a vote.
You will hear it in your own head: 'I paid for it', 'I have come this far', 'I can't stop now'. Each one is the past asking to vote. Let it speak, then decide on the future.

cards.question: What's the right question when you're 20 minutes into a bad movie?
choices: Was the ticket worth the $15 I paid for it?
Is the next 90 minutes of my evening worth it?
How much did the ticket cost compared to usual?
cards.why: The ticket is spent whatever you do. The only thing you still control is the time ahead.

title: Confirmation bias
blurb: Your brain lets in what agrees with you and waves off what doesn't. You'll see the filter at work, and the one question that gets around it.
takeaway: You learned to look for what would prove you wrong.

cards.body: Facts come at you all day. Some fit what you already think. Some don't.
The ones that fit sail through. They feel obviously true, so you remember them.
The ones that don't fit get a harder look, a shrug, or no look at all. You forget them by dinner.
So you end up more sure, not more right. The only way around it is to go looking for the fact that would prove you wrong.
You think your friend is mad at you. You'll notice the short text and miss the two normal ones. Ask instead: what would I see if they weren't?
You don't test beliefs by finding support. You test them by hunting for the thing that would break them.

cards.question: What's the best way to check whether a belief is true?
choices: Collect examples that support it
Look for what would disprove it
Ask people who agree with you
cards.why: Support is easy to find for almost anything. A belief that survives a real attempt to break it has earned something.

title: Nobody is watching you that closely
blurb: The spotlight effect: you feel like everyone noticed, and they didn't. You'll see the study where people overestimated by half, and why it happens.
takeaway: You learned that everyone is in their own spotlight.

cards.body: You walk in wearing something embarrassing. It feels like a spotlight is on you and the whole room is looking.
But everyone else is standing in their own spotlight. They're busy with how they look.
In a famous study, students wore an embarrassing shirt into a room. They guessed half the room noticed. About a quarter actually did.
You overestimate by about double. The stumble, the wrong answer, the bad haircut. Half the people you think saw it didn't.
You are the main character of your day only. Everyone else is the main character of theirs.

cards.question: How many people noticed the embarrassing shirt, compared to the guess?
choices: About the same
About half as many
About twice as many
cards.why: Students guessed around half the room. About a quarter noticed. We overrate how much others see.

title: The habit loop
blurb: Every habit has three parts, and only one of them is the part you see. You'll find the cue and reward hiding around a habit, and learn to swap the middle instead of fighting all three.
takeaway: You learned to swap the routine, not fight the loop.

cards.body: A habit is a loop with three parts. It runs on its own, without you deciding anything, which is why it's so hard to fight head on.
Cue, routine, reward. Round and round. Every habit you have, good or bad, runs on this same loop. Once you can see the parts, you can work on it.
The cue is the trigger. You sit down on your bed after school, bag still on. Nothing has happened yet, but the loop has already started.
The routine is what you do. Phone out, feed open, thumb moving. It is the only part of the loop you actually notice, so it gets all the blame.
The reward is what you get. Twenty minutes of not thinking about anything. The loop runs to get this, and it will run again tomorrow.
You can't delete a cue or a reward. The bed is still there and you still need the break. But you can swap what happens in the middle.
Same bed. Same twenty minutes off. Different thing in your hand. A book, a sketchpad, a guitar. The loop still gets its reward, so it keeps running.
Bedtime scroll, after-class snack, the coffee you need before you can start anything. All loops, all built the same way. Look for the three parts.
Next time the habit fires, stop and ask three things. Where are you, what time is it, what just happened. That is the cue, and now you can see it coming.
Keep the cue. Keep the reward. Swap only the routine in between.

cards.question: Which part of the loop can you actually change?
choices: The cue, by avoiding the places and times that trigger it.
The routine, what you do between the trigger and the payoff.
The reward, by training yourself to stop wanting the payoff.
cards.why: Cues and rewards are wired in. The bed is still there and you still want the break. The routine in the middle is the part you get to pick.

title: Say 'I'm excited', not 'calm down'
blurb: Nerves and excitement feel the same in the body. You'll see why 'calm down' fails, and the two words that turned a racing heart into a better test score.
takeaway: You learned to relabel nerves instead of fighting them.

cards.body: Racing heart. Sweaty hands. Fast breathing. Your body does exactly this before a test, a speech, or a first date.
Call it anxiety and your brain reads it as a threat. Now you're nervous about being nervous.
Call it excitement and nothing in the body changes. Same heart rate, same hands. Only the label moved.
'Calm down' asks your body to do the impossible. 'I'm excited' asks it to do nothing. That's why it works.
In one study, people said either 'I'm calm' or 'I'm excited' before singing karaoke. The excited group scored about 80%. The calm group scored about 53%.
Your body can't tell nervous from excited. So tell it which one it is.

cards.question: Why does 'I'm excited' beat 'calm down'?
choices: It slows your heart
It changes the label, not the body
It distracts you
cards.why: The racing heart stays. Calling it excitement stops you fighting it and points the energy somewhere useful.

title: Ask for an extension the right way
blurb: Teachers say yes to a good extension email far more often than students think. You'll build the four-line version: what, when, the specific ask, and proof you've started.
takeaway: You learned the four lines that get a yes.

cards.body: An extension email has four lines. Send it before the deadline, not after. That one detail changes the answer more than anything else.
Line one: what and when. 'The bio lab report is due Friday.' No story yet.
Line two: the ask, with a date. 'Could I turn it in Monday at 8am?' A specific date is easy to say yes to. 'A few more days' is not.
Line three: proof you've started. 'I've attached my draft with the first two sections done.' This is what separates you from the ones who haven't begun.
Line four: thanks, and stop. No paragraph about why. If they want the reason, they'll ask.
Ask early. Name a date. Show the draft. Skip the story.

cards.question: Which detail matters most in an extension request?
choices: A detailed reason
Sending it before the due date
Apologising a lot
cards.why: Before the deadline it's a request. After, it's an excuse. Teachers treat the two very differently.

title: How to say no
blurb: A clean no is short, kind, and doesn't invite a negotiation. You'll see the three-part shape, and why a long excuse is the thing that gets you talked back into it.
takeaway: You learned that a short no is the kind one.

cards.body: Saying no feels rude, so most people bury it in a long excuse. The excuse is the problem, not the no. A clean no is short, kind, and does not invite a negotiation.
A clean no has three parts. Something warm. The no, plain. And, if you want it, what you can do instead. That is the whole shape.
Something warm. 'Thanks for thinking of me.' It is true, and it costs nothing. It tells them the no is about the request, not about them.
The no, plain. 'I can't this weekend.' No 'maybe', no 'I'll try', no 'let me see'. A soft no gets treated as a yes.
If you want it: what you can do. 'But I'm free Tuesday.' Now it is an offer, not a rejection. Skip it if you do not mean it.
What you leave out: the reason. Every reason is a door. 'I have homework' gets 'do it after'. 'I'm tired' gets 'just for an hour'. No reason, no door.
Here is one in full, by text. Warm, no, offer. Sixteen words. It reads as kind because it is short, not in spite of it.
If they push, say the same no again, in the same words, with the same warmth. You do not need a new reason. The second no is easier than the first.
The guilt fades in about a minute. The resentment from a yes you did not mean lasts the whole weekend. Short no now, or long yes later.
Warm, then no, then an offer. The excuse is what gets you talked back in.

cards.question: Why skip the reason when you say no?
choices: Giving a reason comes across as rude to them.
Every reason is something they can argue with.
It makes you look busier than you really are.
cards.why: A reason turns your no into a problem to solve. 'I have homework' invites 'do it later'. A plain no has nothing to push on.

title: Listen so people feel heard
blurb: When a friend is upset, the instinct is to fix it or cheer them up. Both make it worse. You'll learn the one move that works: say back what you heard, then ask.
takeaway: You learned to reflect before you fix.

cards.body: A friend says: 'I completely bombed that test.' What you say next decides whether they keep talking.
'You'll be fine' feels kind. It isn't. It tells them the feeling was wrong, and the conversation ends.
Try saying back what you heard: 'Sounds like it really got to you.' Nothing fixed. Nothing judged. They feel heard, and they keep going.
Then ask, don't advise. 'What part went wrong?' Advice comes later, if they want it. Most of the time they don't.
Reflect it back. Then ask. Fixing can wait, and usually isn't wanted.

cards.question: A friend says they bombed a test. What's the best first reply?
choices: 'You'll be fine, you always are'
'Sounds like it really got to you'
'Next time start studying earlier'
cards.why: Saying back what you heard shows you listened. The other two close the conversation, one with comfort and one with a lecture.

title: Small talk without the panic
blurb: You don't need good stories. You need follow-up questions. You'll see the ladder that turns 'where are you from' into a real conversation, and the study on why askers get liked.
takeaway: You learned that follow-ups do the work.

cards.body: Small talk feels hard because you think you need something interesting to say. You don't. You need the next question.
Start anywhere. 'Where are you from?' Boring is fine. It's the bottom rung, not the whole ladder.
Then climb: ask about their answer. 'What do you like about it?' Now they're talking about something they care about.
Climb again. 'How did you get into that?' Three rungs in, it's a real conversation, and you've said almost nothing.
Researchers watched hundreds of first conversations. The people who asked more follow-up questions were consistently rated more likeable.
You don't need a good story. You need the next question about theirs.

cards.question: What made people more likeable in first conversations?
choices: Telling better stories
Asking follow-up questions
Talking about shared interests
cards.why: Follow-up questions show you listened to the last answer. That's what people remember, not your stories.

title: A real apology has three parts
blurb: 'Sorry you feel that way' isn't an apology, and everyone can tell. You'll see the three parts a real one needs, and the two words that quietly cancel it.
takeaway: You learned what makes 'sorry' land.

cards.body: A real apology has three parts. Most people do one part, usually the word 'sorry', and then wonder why it did not work. Here is what the other two are.
What I did. What it cost you. What changes. Say all three, in that order, and the apology lands. Skip one and it wobbles.
Name what you did. 'I told people what you said in private.' Specific. Say the actual thing. No 'if I did anything' and no 'mistakes were made'.
Name what it cost them. 'That made it hard to trust me.' This is the part people skip, and the part that matters most. It shows you understand.
Say what changes. 'I'm not going to repeat things you tell me.' An apology with no change in it is just a description of what happened.
Two words cancel all of it: 'but' and 'if'. 'I'm sorry, but' means 'I'm not sorry'. 'Sorry if you were hurt' means 'this is your problem'.
Here is one in full, by text. Three parts, no but, no if, no excuses. It is short. A good apology usually is.
'Sorry you feel that way' is not an apology. It names their feeling instead of your action. Everyone can tell, even if they cannot say why.
Then stop talking. Do not ask to be forgiven right away, and do not explain why you did it. The other person gets to decide what happens next.
What I did. What it cost you. What changes. No but, no if.

cards.question: What does 'I'm sorry if you were hurt' actually say?
choices: That you own what you did and plan to change it.
That the hurt is their problem, not your action.
That you are sorry but unsure of what happened.
cards.why: 'If' puts the feeling in doubt. It sounds like an apology, but it doesn't own anything.

title: Where your paycheck goes
blurb: Your first paycheck is smaller than the number you agreed to. You'll see exactly who takes what from $1,000, and why some of it comes back in April.
takeaway: You learned the difference between gross and take-home.

cards.body: You earn $1,000 in a month. That is your gross pay, the number on the offer. It is not what lands in your account. Something takes a bite first, and it helps to know who.
Here is the whole split of $1,000 at a glance. Two fixed bites for Social Security and Medicare, one that varies for income tax, and the rest is yours.
Social Security takes 6.2%. That is $62 of the $1,000. It funds monthly payments to people who are retired now, and one day, to you.
Medicare takes 1.45%. That is $14.50. Together with Social Security these are called FICA, 7.65% of every paycheck, and almost every worker pays them.
Income tax varies. It depends on the W-4 form you fill in on day one and on your state. For a student earning this little, it is often $0 to $100 of the $1,000.
What is left is your net pay, or take-home. Around $825 to $925 of the $1,000. Gross is what you earned. Net is what you get.
If too much income tax was taken during the year, you get it back after you file in April. A refund is not a gift. It is your own money coming home late.
Your pay stub lists every line. Gross at the top, each bite in the middle, net at the bottom. Read the first one you get. After that you will never be surprised again.
Your employer pays another 7.65% on top, matching your FICA. It never shows on your stub, but it is part of what you cost them, and part of what the job is worth.
Gross is what you earned. Net is what you get. The gap is FICA plus income tax.

cards.question: Which of these does every worker pay, no matter what?
choices: State income tax on every paycheck.
Social Security and Medicare, called FICA.
A refund at the end of the tax year.
cards.why: FICA comes off almost every paycheck at fixed rates. Income tax depends on your state and your form, and some people owe none.

title: Tax brackets aren't what you think
blurb: Moving into a higher bracket never costs you money. You'll see how brackets work like stacked buckets, and why a raise is always worth taking.
takeaway: You learned that only the top slice pays the top rate.

cards.body: Everyone has heard it: do not take the raise, it will push you into a higher bracket and you will take home less. It is wrong, and a picture of stacked buckets shows why.
Tax brackets are stacked buckets. Your taxable income, your pay minus the standard deduction, fills them from the bottom up. Each bucket has its own rate.
The first $11,925 you earn is taxed at 10%. That is the bottom bucket, and everyone's first dollars go here, whether they earn $20,000 or $2 million.
The next chunk, up to $48,475, is taxed at 12%. Only the money in this bucket pays 12%. The bottom bucket still pays 10%. Nothing below it moves.
Above that, up to $103,350, the rate is 22%. Have $50,000 of taxable income and only $1,525 of it is in this bucket. The rest sits in the cheaper ones below.
So $50,000 of taxable income does not pay 22% of $50,000. It pays $1,193, plus $4,386, plus $336. About $5,900 in total, not $11,000. Under 12% overall.
A raise that pushes you into a higher bracket only taxes the new dollars at the higher rate. You never take home less by earning more. Take the raise.
Taxable income is smaller than your pay. The standard deduction takes $15,000 off the top first, for a single filer in 2025. Earn $60,000 and only $45,000 goes into the buckets.
Knowing the buckets kills the fear. A raise is a raise. A bonus is a bonus. The only number that matters is the one at the bottom of the stub, and it only goes up.
Only the dollars above the line pay the higher rate. A raise never costs you money.

cards.question: You have $50,000 of taxable income and the 22% bracket starts at $48,475. How much is taxed at 22%?
choices: All $50,000, once you cross the line.
About $1,500, the part above the line.
None of it until you reach $103,350.
cards.why: Only the money above the bracket line, about $1,525, pays 22%. Everything below it stays in the cheaper buckets.

title: A Roth IRA at 18
blurb: It's a jar where money grows for decades and comes out with no tax at all. You'll see why starting at 18 beats starting at 30 by a mile, and the one rule for opening one.
takeaway: You learned why the early jar wins.

cards.body: A Roth IRA is a jar for retirement money. Money you already paid tax on goes in. Then it sits and grows for decades, and the growth is never taxed.
Inside the jar, growth is never taxed. One $2,000 deposit at 18 becomes about $48,000 by 65 at 7% a year, and you owe nothing on the extra $46,000.
After 59½, and once the account is five years old, it all comes out tax-free. The money you put in, not the growth, can come out any time without penalty.
You need earned income. A summer job counts. Babysitting money counts if you report it. You can put in up to $7,000 a year, or everything you earned if that is less.
Put in $2,000 a year from 18 to 24, then stop forever. That is $14,000 in, and about $277,000 at 65. Start at 30 and you need $2,000 every year until 65, $70,000 in, to land in the same place.
Any big brokerage will open one online in about fifteen minutes. There is no minimum at most of them. Pick a plain index fund inside it and stop touching it.
A Roth IRA is the jar, not the thing inside. You still choose what goes in it. For most people that is one broad index fund. The jar just keeps the tax off.
The jar rewards years, not amounts. Seven years at 18 can match thirty-five years starting at 30, because the early money has four extra decades to double.
Set it to automatic. $167 a month is $2,000 a year. If that is too much, $50 a month still counts. The habit matters more than the amount at 18.
The jar rewards years, not amounts. Seven years at 18 can match thirty-five years later.

cards.question: What do you need before you can open a Roth IRA?
choices: To be at least 21 years old.
Money you earned from work.
A full-time job with benefits.
cards.why: Any earned income counts, including a summer job. Age and hours don't matter, only that the money came from work.

title: Why a dollar shrinks
blurb: Inflation is why the burrito that cost $8 now costs $10. You'll see what that does to cash sitting still, and why a savings account has to beat it to keep up.
takeaway: You learned why cash sitting still loses.

cards.body: In 2020 this burrito cost $8. Same burrito, same place, same person behind the counter. Keep that $8 in your head for a moment.
In 2025 it costs about $10. Prices across almost everything rose roughly a quarter in those five years. That is inflation: not one shop being greedy, but the whole price level moving.
Your $8 did not change. But now it buys about four-fifths of a burrito. The number on the bill stayed the same. The dollar got smaller.
Cash under a mattress loses around 3% of its buying power a year, in a normal year. It looks safe because the number never moves. That is exactly the problem.
A savings account paying 4% stays a bit ahead of prices. One paying 0.1% does not. Over ten years the gap between those two is the difference between keeping up and quietly falling behind.
A little inflation is normal and mostly planned. Central banks aim for about 2% a year. Your grandparents' story about the movie that cost a quarter is the same story, told from the other end.
Keep $500 in cash for five years at 3% inflation and it buys what $430 buys today. The bills still say $500. The shelf disagrees.
This is why a raise that only matches inflation is not a raise. If prices rose 3% and your pay rose 3%, you can buy exactly what you could last year. Nothing more.
Keep this month's money in cash. Keep this year's in a savings account that pays close to inflation. Anything you will not touch for years goes where it can grow faster than prices.
A dollar is a claim on stuff. If stuff gets pricier, the dollar gets smaller.

cards.question: You keep $500 in cash for five years. What happens to it?
choices: Nothing, it is still exactly $500 in the drawer.
It buys less than it did when you put it there.
It grows a little, because cash earns a bit too.
cards.why: The bills say $500, but prices went up around it. The same cash buys fewer burritos than it did.

title: The trolley problem
blurb: A runaway trolley, five people, one lever. You'll see why almost everyone pulls it, why almost nobody pushes, and why that gap is the question behind self-driving cars and every triage rule.
takeaway: You learned that how a harm happens changes the answer, even when the count doesn't.

cards.body: A runaway trolley is coming down the track. The brakes are gone, and it is not slowing down. Nobody on board can stop it.
Ahead, the track splits in two. Which way the trolley goes depends on a lever beside the track. Right now it points down the main line.
On the main track: five people. They can’t get out of the way. If nobody does anything, the trolley hits all five.
On the side track: one person, just as stuck. And you’re standing at the lever. You have a few seconds to decide.
Pull it, and the trolley turns. One person dies instead of five. Ask a room full of people and most of them say the same thing: pull.
It feels like simple math. Five is more than one, so you save the five. Now change one detail and watch how fast that math stops working.
Same trolley. Same five people. But now you’re on a bridge over the track, next to a large stranger. The only way to stop the trolley is to push him off, into its path.
Still one death instead of five. The math hasn’t changed at all. But almost nobody says they would push. Something else is going on.
At the lever, the one person dies because of where he was standing. A side effect. On the bridge, you use the man to stop the trolley. He’s the tool.
Five versus one is the easy part. What we actually argue about is whether a person was used.
This isn’t just a puzzle. A self-driving car has to be told what to do when a crash can’t be avoided. Someone writes that rule.
An emergency room decides who gets treated first when there isn’t time for everyone. Same argument, no lever. Real people.

cards.question: A surgeon could save five patients using the organs of one healthy visitor. Almost everyone says no. Which case is this most like?
choices: The lever. One life is traded for five, so the math is the same.
The bridge. The visitor is used as the means to save the five.
Neither. Medicine has its own rules, so the cases don’t compare.
cards.why: The numbers match the lever, but the visitor isn’t in the way of anything. He’s the tool that saves the five. That is exactly what the bridge case tests.

title: The ship of Theseus
blurb: Replace every plank on a ship, one at a time. Is it the same ship? You'll see the puzzle, the twist that makes it worse, and why your phone and your body are in it too.
takeaway: You learned that 'same' is a choice, not a fact.

cards.body: The Greeks kept the hero Theseus's ship in the harbour at Athens for centuries as a monument. Wood rots. So they replaced the planks as they went.
One plank at a time. After a while, a third of the ship is new wood. Still his ship? Sure, it feels like it. Nobody would argue.
Eventually every plank has been swapped. Not one piece of the original is left. Same ship? Same name, same harbour, same shape. But nothing he touched.
Someone saved all the old planks and rebuilt them into a second ship. Now there are two. One has the history. One has the material. Which one is Theseus's?
Each ship has a real claim. The first never stopped being the ship. The second is made of the ship. 'Same' cannot mean both at once, and that is the puzzle.
Your phone with a new screen, a new battery, and a new back. Same phone? You would say yes. It has your photos and your cracked case. The parts were never the point.
Most of the cells in your body get replaced over the years. The you in the childhood photo shares almost no material with the you holding it. Same you? Obviously. And also, a puzzle.
'Same' is not a fact about the thing. It is a rule we choose. Same by history, or same by material. Pick the rule, and the puzzle answers itself. The ship was never confused.
A band with no original members. A company with a new logo, staff and product. A team that moved cities. Every argument about whether it is 'really' the same is this ship.
Same is not a fact about the thing. It's a rule we choose. Pick the rule, and the puzzle answers itself.

cards.question: Why is the rebuilt ship of old planks such a problem?
choices: Old wood is weaker and it will not float.
Two ships can each claim to be the original.
Nobody remembers which plank came first.
cards.why: One ship has the history. The other has the material. Each has a real claim, and 'same' can't mean both.

title: Plato's cave
blurb: Prisoners chained to a wall, watching shadows, sure the shadows are the world. You'll see the oldest thought experiment about what's real, and why walking out hurts.
takeaway: You learned why leaving the cave hurts before it helps.

cards.body: Picture people chained in a cave since birth, facing the back wall. They cannot turn their heads. All they have ever seen is that wall.
On the wall, shadows move. To the prisoners, the shadows are the world. They name them, predict which comes next, and argue about who is right.
Behind them, a fire. Between the fire and the prisoners, people walk past carrying objects. The shadows are just those objects. The prisoners have never seen a real one.
One prisoner gets loose. He turns around and sees the fire, and the objects that made the shadows. It hurts to look. His first instinct is to turn back to the wall.
He climbs the passage out. The sunlight is blinding. Everything looks wrong at first. It takes time before he can look at real things, and longer to look at the sun.
When he comes back to explain, his eyes cannot see in the dark anymore. He stumbles. The others decide the trip ruined him. Nobody else wants to leave.
A feed shows you a version of people: highlights, arguments, the worst clip of someone's day. It is easy to forget those are shadows of people, not the people.
Plato's point is about knowing. Shadows are what you are shown. Objects are what is really there. The sun is why. Most of us live one step up from the wall, at best.
Leaving the cave always hurts first. The new thing looks wrong, the old thing looks safe, and the people still inside think you have changed. That is the price of looking.
The first taste of something real feels worse than the shadow. That's not a sign you were wrong to look.

cards.question: Why do the prisoners think the freed one has gone mad?
choices: He is lying to them about what he saw outside.
The shadows are all they have ever known as real.
He cannot describe the sun in words they know.
cards.why: The shadows are their whole world. Anyone claiming there's something more real must be broken.

title: Notes you'll actually reread
blurb: Most notes get written once and never opened. You'll set up a page with three zones, so the notes quiz you later instead of just sitting there.
takeaway: You learned to make notes that test you.

cards.body: One page, three zones. Draw the lines before class starts. A wide zone on the right, a thin column on the left, a strip along the bottom. Ten seconds.
The big zone on the right is for class. Write what is said, fast and messy. Do not fix it live. Neat can wait. Catching it cannot.
The thin column on the left is for after class. Turn each chunk of notes into a question. 'What does the mitochondria do?' Ten minutes, the same day.
The strip at the bottom is one sentence that sums up the page. If you cannot write it, you did not get the class yet. Useful to know on Tuesday, not in the exam.
Cover the right side. Read the questions on the left. Answer out loud. Uncover and check. That is a quiz you built yourself, from your own class.
Notes that cannot quiz you are just a transcript. You will never reread a transcript. You will reread a page that asks you things.
A Cornell professor, Walter Pauk, designed it in the 1950s for students who took pages of notes and never opened them again. It has not needed changing since.
Write in class. Add the questions the same day, while you still remember what the scribble meant. Quiz yourself a week later. Three touches, one page.
By the end of term you have a notebook that is also a question bank. Revision is reading the left column and checking the right. No new material to make.
Notes that can't quiz you are just a transcript. Add the question column.

cards.question: What goes in the left column?
choices: A neat rewritten copy of the class notes.
Questions that the notes on the right answer.
The page numbers of the matching textbook.
cards.why: The left column turns the page into a test. Cover the right side and the questions are all you see.

title: Explain it to a twelve-year-old
blurb: If you can't explain it simply, you don't know it yet. You'll use a blank page and plain words to find exactly where your understanding runs out.
takeaway: You learned where your understanding runs out.

cards.body: Take a blank page. Write the topic at the top. Photosynthesis, say. Then explain it in words a twelve-year-old would follow, with no terms you would have to define.
'The plant catches sunlight and uses it to turn air and water into sugar.' That is the whole idea in one plain line. If you can write that line, you have it.
Keep going until you hit a spot where the words go vague. 'And then it... does something with the light?' That is the gap. That is the exact thing you do not know yet.
Go back to the textbook for that one gap only. Fill it, then rewrite the sentence plainly. Repeat until there is no vague spot left.
Explain, find the vague spot, look it up, explain again. Each lap the vague spots get fewer. When there are none, you are done. Not before.
Richard Feynman, a physicist, was famous for explaining hard things in plain words. He said if you cannot explain it simply, you do not understand it well enough. This is his method.
A real twelve-year-old is better than an imaginary one. A younger sibling, a cousin, a friend who does not take the class. They ask the question you skipped.
'Chlorophyll absorbs photons for the light-dependent reactions' can be said by someone who understands nothing. 'The green stuff catches the light' cannot. Big words hide gaps. Plain words find them.
You are done when you can say it to a friend in one breath with no terms and no pauses. Try it before every test. It takes a minute per topic and finds every hole.
Big words hide gaps. Plain words find them.

cards.question: What does it mean when your explanation goes vague?
choices: You need a bigger, more precise word there.
You found the exact thing you do not know yet.
The topic is too hard to explain simply.
cards.why: Vague words are where understanding runs out. That spot tells you what to go back and learn.

title: Sleep is part of studying
blurb: Your brain files what you learned while you sleep. You'll see what happens in the early and late hours of the night, and why an all-nighter throws away the studying you did.
takeaway: You learned that the night does the filing.

cards.body: You study, then you sleep. Most people think the learning stopped when the book closed. It did not. Some of the most important part is about to happen.
Sleep runs in cycles, about ninety minutes each. Five or so in a full night. The early cycles and the late cycles do different jobs.
The deep sleep comes early in the night. The best evidence says this is when the day's facts get moved from short-term storage into long-term. The filing shift.
The dream-heavy sleep comes late. This is when the brain connects new things to what you already knew. The part that turns facts into understanding.
Cut the night to four hours and you keep the filing but lose the connecting. Skip the night and you lose both. Studying at 3am is writing to a drive that will not save.
The all-nighter feels productive because you are awake and the pages are turning. The facts you cram after midnight never get moved into storage. You read them. They do not stick.

In a 1924 study, people who learned a list and then slept remembered about half of it eight hours later. People who learned it and stayed awake remembered about one in ten. Same hours, one difference.
The night before a test is not the time to cram. It is the time to sleep, so the week's studying gets filed. Review for twenty minutes, then close the book and let the brain finish.
Move the studying earlier in the week. Sleep full nights, especially the last two. The night before, a short review and an early lights-out. Sleep is the last step, not the break.
Sleep isn't the break from studying. It's the last step of it.

cards.question: What does an all-nighter before a test cost you?
choices: Nothing much, if you drink enough coffee.
The filing your brain does while you sleep.
Only your mood and your focus in the morning.
cards.why: The facts you crammed never get moved to long-term storage. You read them, but they don't stick.

title: The first minute of a test
blurb: Most people start on question one and run out of time on question eight. You'll spend the first sixty seconds differently, and get the easy points before the hard ones eat the clock.
takeaway: You learned to spend the first minute looking, not writing.

cards.body: The test lands on your desk. Do not touch question one yet. The first minute decides how the next fifty go, and most people spend it on the wrong thing.
Spend sixty seconds reading every question. Just reading. Now you know what is coming, roughly how long you have per point, and where the easy ones are.
Do the ones you are sure about first. Every easy point is worth the same as a hard one, and it is yours in two minutes instead of ten.
Mark the hard ones and skip them. Not stuck, just later. Coming back fresh, with the easy points banked, often makes a hard one look smaller.
Fifty minutes: one to read, thirty for the ones you know, the rest for the hard ones. The order protects the points you were always going to get.
One student spends fifteen minutes on question one and runs out of time on three easy ones at the end. The other banks the easy ones and comes back. Same knowledge, ten points apart.
Come back with the time you have left, and with the easy points already banked. A hard question you run out of time on costs nothing now. It was a bonus.
Circle the question number and write one word next to it: 'later', or the method you think it wants. When you come back, the word saves you the reread.
This is also how you stop panicking. A test you have already read is a known thing. The first minute buys calm for the other forty-nine.
Skim it all. Bank the easy points. Then spend what's left on the hard ones.

cards.question: Why skip a hard question instead of pushing through it?
choices: Hard questions are worth fewer points anyway.
It stops the hard one eating time from easy ones.
You will never get the hard one no matter what.
cards.why: A hard question can eat ten minutes and three easy questions with it. Bank the easy ones first, then come back.

title: Why $900 feels cheap
blurb: The first price you see quietly sets what every price after it feels like. It's called anchoring, and you'll watch it move the same jacket by $450.
takeaway: You learned that the first number drags every number after it.

cards.body: Two stores. Same jacket. The only difference is which price you happen to see first.
At Store A the first tag you see says $1,200. You haven't looked at the jacket yet. That number is already in your head.
Ask what you'd pay for the jacket and you land near $900. Not cheap. Just cheaper than the number already in your head.
Store B has the same jacket. The first tag here is $300. Now $450 feels like plenty to pay.
Same jacket, two answers, $450 apart. Nothing changed but the number you saw first.

Researchers spun a wheel, then asked people about the countries in the UN. Is the share of them in Africa higher or lower than the wheel's number? Then they had to name the real share. People who saw 65 guessed about 45%. People who saw 10 guessed about 25%.
The first number is not information. It's an anchor someone else dropped. Bring your own before you look.

cards.question: You're asking for pay at a summer job. Who ends up setting the range?
choices: Whoever says a number first
Whoever talks longer
Whoever needs it more
cards.why: The first number said out loud becomes the spot everyone argues around. So have your own number ready before you hear theirs.

title: Why they're a jerk and you're just busy
blurb: Their mistake means they're careless, but your mistake means it was a bad week. You'll see why the same act lands in two different boxes, and the one question that evens it out.
takeaway: You learned that you judge them by what they did, and yourself by what you meant.

cards.body: Something goes wrong. Your brain has two boxes to put the cause in. The person, or the situation. Every explanation lands in one of them.
A classmate snaps at you in the hall. You file it under person. They're rude. That's the box you reach for first.
